# Registered report: Discovery and preclinical validation of drug indications using compendia of public gene expression data

## Authors

- Irawati Kandela<sup>1</sup>
- Ioannis Zervantonakis<sup>2</sup>

### Affiliations

1. Developmental Therapeutics Core Northwestern University, Evanston Illinois United States
2. Harvard Medical School, Boston Massachusetts United States

† Corresponding author

## Abstract

10.7554/eLife.06847.001 The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012. This Registered report describes the proposed replication plan of key experiments from ‘Discovery and Preclinical Validation of Drug Indications Using Compendia of Public Gene Expression Data’ by Sirota et al., published in Science Translational Medicine in 2011 ( Sirota et al., 2011 ). The key experiments being replicated include Figure 4C and D and Supplemental Figure 1. In these figures, Sirota and colleagues. tested a proof of concept experiment validating their prediction that cimetidine, a histamine-2 (H2) receptor agonist commonly used to treat peptic ulcers ( Kubecova et al., 2011 ), would be effective against lung adenocarcinoma (Figure 4C and D). As a control they also tested the effects of cimetidine against renal carcinoma, for which it was not predicted to be efficacious (Supplemental Figure 1). The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is a collaboration between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange , and the results of the replications will be published by eLife . DOI: http://dx.doi.org/10.7554/eLife.06847.001

## Introduction

In this paper, Sirota and colleagues tested their hypothesis that extant drugs could be repurposed to target alternative diseases; if so, this could improve efficiency in the search for new treatments. They compared data from the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO)—which they used to determine gene expression signatures of diseases—to data from the Connectivity Map, which tracks the changes in mRNA expression caused by 164 drugs. By comparing these two mRNA expression sets, Sirota and colleagues created a similarity score to describe how similar the changes in mRNA expression were between each drug and each disease. They theorized that a similarity score close to −1 (exactly opposite signatures) might indicate that the drug could treat the disease.

In Figure 4C and D, Sirota and colleagues directly test their hypothesis by examining the effects of cimetidine, an H2 receptor blocker commonly used to treat gastric ulcers by reducing the production of stomach acid (Kubecova et al., 2011), on xenograft transplanted A549 lung adenocarcinoma cells. Mice treated with cimetidine showed a dose-dependent reduction in tumor size after 12 days of treatment. In Supplemental Figure 1, they also treated ACHN renal carcinoma cells with cimetidine, although cimetidine was not predicted to treat this cancer line. They observed no effect of cimetidine on the growth of this cancer cell line. These experiments will be replicated in Protocol 1. However, the conclusions that can be drawn from these experiments are limited by the fact that only a single cell line was tested with only a single drug.

To date, no direct replication of the experiments presented in Sirota and colleagues' Figure 4C and D or Supplemental Figure 1 has been reported. However, Stoyanov and colleagues did examine the effect of cimetidine on growth of A459 cells activated with histamine and reported that cimetidine did reduce proliferation in vitro (Stoyanov et al., 2012). An exploratory analysis of a cohort of diabetic patients demonstrated a decreased risk of developing lung cancer, specifically adenocarcinoma, in patients who took over-the-counter H2 receptor blockers, including cimetidine (Hsu et al., 2013).

## Materials and methods

Unless otherwise noted, all protocol information was derived from the original paper, references from the original paper, or information obtained directly from the authors. An asterisk (*) indicates data or information provided by the Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology core team. A hashtag (#) indicates information provided by the replicating lab.

## Protocol 1: assessing the effect of cimetidine treatment on tumor growth in a xenograft model of lung carcinoma and a xenograft model of renal carcinoma

This protocol describes how to create xenograft tumors in severe combined immunodeficient (SCID) mice from A549 lung carcinoma cells (as seen in Figure 4C and D) or ACHN renal carcinoma cells (Supplemental Figure 1). Tumor growth is then assessed during 11 days of cimetidine treatment. Sirota and colleagues designed this experiment to test their predictions that A549 cells would be susceptible to cimetidine treatment while ACHN cells would not. Treatment with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) alone will serve as the negative control, while treatment with the lung adenocarcinoma standard drug doxorubicin will serve as the positive control.

## Sampling

This experiment will use at least 12 mice per group for a final power of 82.4%.See ‘Power calculations’ for details.The experiment contains five cohorts total:A549 lung adenocarcinoma xenografts:a. Cohort 1: mice treated with PBS (negative control).i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.b. Cohort 2: mice treated with 2 mg/kg doxorubicin (Dox) (positive control).i. N = 5.■ To ensure at least 3 tumors develop.c. Cohort 3: mice treated with 100 mg/kg cimetidine.i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.ACHN renal carcinoma xenografts:a. Cohort 1: mice treated with PBS (negative control).i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.b. Cohort 2: mice treated with 100 mg/kg cimetidine.i. N = 14.■ To ensure at least 12 tumors develop.

## Deliverables

Data to be collected:Mouse health records, including age and tumor volume at start of injections, time of tumor detection, any excluded mice (including reason for exclusion).Raw data of tumor dimensions by day.Final weight of tumors.Graph of relative mean tumor weight in each cohort starting on Day 1 post-100 mm3 (as seen in Figure 4C and Supplemental Figure 1).a. Normalize Day 2 onwards to the weight at Day 1.Image of all tumors alongside ruler (as seen in Figure 4D) for both A459 xenografts and ACHN xenografts.

## Confirmatory analysis plan

Statistical analysis of replication data:At the time of analysis, we will perform the Shapiro–Wilk test and generate a quantile–quantile (q–q) plot to attempt to assess the normality of the data and also perform Levene's test to assess homoscedasiticity. If the data appear skewed, we will attempt a transformation in order to proceed with the proposed statistical analysis listed below and possibly perform the appropriate non-parametric test.a. Comparison of the mean relative tumor weight of 100 mg/kg cimetidine treatment at day 11 as compared to PBS treatment at day 11 for both A549 and ACHN xenograft tumors.i. Two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) (2 × 2 factorial) followed by Bonferroni corrected Welch's t-tests for the following comparisons:■ PBS-treated A549 tumors vs cimetidine-treated A459 tumors.■ PBS-treated ACHN tumors vs cimetidine-treated ACHN tumors.ii. Additional comparison of PBS-treated A459 tumors to doxorubicin-treated tumors.■Bonferroni corrected Welch's t-test outside the framework of the ANOVA.Meta-analysis of original and replication attempt effect sizes:This replication attempt will perform the statistical analysis listed above, compute the effects sizes, compare them against the reported effect size in the original paper and use a meta-analytic approach to combine the original and replication effects, which will be presented as a forest plot.

## Known differences from the original study

The replication attempt will encompass the PBS control, the doxorubicin control and the highest dose of cimetidine (100 mg/kg). It will not include the 25 mg/ml or 50 mg/ml cimetidine treatment groups.While the original study performed injections of 5 × 106 cells per microliter of PBS, on the advice of the replicating lab we will inject the same number of cells but suspended in 100 µl PBS.

## Provisions for quality control

Mice will be randomly assigned to xenograft model and treatment type. All data obtained from the experiment—raw data, data analysis, control data and quality control data—will be made publicly available, either in the published manuscript or as an open access dataset available on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/hxrmm/).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.06847.002](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.06847.002)

eLife posts the editorial decision letter and author response on a selection of the published articles (subject to the approval of the authors). An edited version of the letter sent to the authors after peer review is shown, indicating the substantive concerns or comments; minor concerns are not usually shown. Reviewers have the opportunity to discuss the decision before the letter is sent (see review process). Similarly, the author response typically shows only responses to the major concerns raised by the reviewers.

Thank you for sending your work entitled “Registered report: Discovery and preclinical validation of drug indications using compendia of public gene expression data” for consideration at eLife. Your article has been favorably evaluated by Stylianos Antonarakis (Senior editor), Chi Dang (Reviewing editor), and 3 reviewers, one of whom is a biostatistician.

The Reviewing editor and the reviewers discussed their comments before we reached this decision, and the Reviewing editor has assembled the following comments to help you prepare a revised submission.

In this study, the authors propose a study to reproduce the findings reported in Figure 4C/D and Supplementary Figure 1 from a previously published manuscript (Sirota et al. Sci Trans Med, 2010), which aimed at assessing the ability to predict drug repurposing opportunities based on connectivity map data analysis. Specifically, the previous Sci Trans Med paper reports that cimetidine, a histamine-2 (H2) receptor agonist commonly used to treat peptic ulcers, can diminish lung cancer tumorigenesis in vivo. There are several key concerns about the design of the study. The first concern is about the duration of the experiment and statistical analysis, and the second about conclusions drawn from using only one lung cancer cell line.

1) At the beginning of the Materials and methods section: The authors plan to follow the mice for 11 days instead of 12 days. Is there a good reason to follow the mice one day short? In addition, the experiment contains five cohorts. Among the five cohorts, cohort 2 only has 5 mice while the other 4 cohorts have 14 mice. Please justify.

2) Power calculation was based on t-test. It is suggested that the authors use two-tailed unequal variance t-test if normality is not violated or the use of Wilcoxon rank-sum test if normality is violated. The authors propose the use of two-way ANOVA followed by t-test for analyzing tumor weight data (in the subsection headed “Confirmatory analysis plan”). Please make sure that the data do not violate the assumptions of ANOVA: normality and homoscedasiticity. If the data do not fit the assumptions well enough, please try to find a data transformation that makes them fit. If this doesn't work, please apply a nonparametric counterpart of ANOVA such as Kruskal–Wallis test. In addition, I suggest the use of contrast within the ANOVA framework instead of t-test if the assumptions of ANOVA are met.

3) To compare growth curves of tumors, the authors propose ANCOVA followed by Bonferroni corrected t-test. Please make sure that the data do not violate the assumptions of ANCOVA and perform transformation or use non-parametric ANCOVA if needed.

4) For the additional comparison of PBS-treated A459 tumors to Doxorubicin treated tumors (in the subsection headed “Confirmatory analysis plan” and in the subsection headed “Test family”), I suggest the use of two-tailed unequal variance t-test instead of t-test if normality is not violated or the use of Wilcoxon rank-sum test if normality is violated.

5) Although the reproducibility project is aimed toward reproducing previously published results, the reviewers would like for the authors to address the limitation of drawing conclusions for the use of only one cell line, A549. Specifically, activity of drugs in cell lines and xenografts is generally highly idiosyncratic. As a result, most journals require that any in vitro and in vivo experiments are replicated in multiple cell lines and in vivo models.

results.result: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is a collaborative initiative between the Center for Open Science and Science Exchange to replicate 50 cancer biology papers published between 2010-2012, with results to be published in eLife.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C6, and C7 provide consistent factual information about the project structure, scope, and publication plan. These are straightforward descriptive claims about the project organization that are internally consistent.

results.result: Sirota et al. (2011) developed a computational approach to drug repurposing by comparing gene expression signatures from the Gene Expression Omnibus with drug-induced expression changes from the Connectivity Map (164 drugs), creating similarity scores where values near -1 suggest therapeutic potential.
results.evaluation: Claims C2 and C8-C12 accurately describe the original study's methodology and hypothesis. The approach is logically sound and the citation is provided. However, the validity of the underlying assumption (that opposite expression signatures indicate therapeutic potential) is not critically evaluated.

results.result: Cimetidine is characterized as both an H2 receptor agonist and an H2 receptor blocker used to treat peptic/gastric ulcers.
results.evaluation: Claims C3 and C13 contain a critical pharmacological error: C3 states cimetidine is an H2 receptor agonist while C13 correctly identifies it as an H2 receptor blocker. These are opposite mechanisms of action. Cimetidine is definitively an H2 receptor antagonist/blocker, not an agonist. This error undermines the accuracy of the manuscript's description of the drug mechanism.

results.result: The original Sirota et al. study demonstrated that cimetidine (100 mg/kg) reduced A549 lung adenocarcinoma xenograft tumor growth (normalized mean weight 2.34 vs 3.3 for PBS at day 11, N=6) but had no effect on ACHN renal carcinoma xenografts (normalized mean weight 2.0 vs 2.14 for PBS, N=6), consistent with computational predictions.
results.evaluation: Claims C4, C5, C14, C15, and C35-C39 consistently describe the original study results with specific quantitative data extracted from figures. The negative control (ACHN) showing no effect strengthens the specificity claim. However, C16 correctly notes the limitation of testing only single cell lines, and the small sample size (N=6) limits statistical power.

results.result: The original experiments are limited by testing only single cell lines with a single drug, though subsequent studies provide partial supporting evidence: Stoyanov et al. (2012) showed cimetidine reduced histamine-activated A549 proliferation in vitro, and Hsu et al. (2013) found decreased lung adenocarcinoma risk in diabetic patients taking H2 blockers.
results.evaluation: Claims C16-C19 appropriately acknowledge experimental limitations and cite relevant follow-up studies. The limitation assessment (C16) is valid given the single cell line design. The supporting studies (C18, C19) provide convergent but not definitive evidence, as they use different experimental systems or are observational.

results.result: The replication protocol specifies detailed experimental procedures including cell culture conditions, xenograft creation (5×10^6 cells in 100 μl PBS), treatment initiation at 100 mm³ tumor volume, 11-day treatment duration, adaptive randomization, and sample sizes (N=14 for PBS/cimetidine groups, N=5 for doxorubicin) to achieve ≥12 evaluable tumors per primary group.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C64 provide comprehensive methodological details that are internally consistent and follow standard xenograft protocols. The adaptive randomization approach (C51) with appropriate covariates is methodologically sound. Quality control measures (C52) are appropriate. Sample size justifications are provided and linked to power calculations.

results.result: The replication differs from the original study by testing only the highest cimetidine dose (100 mg/kg) and using 100 μl PBS injection volume instead of the original 1 μl per 5×10^6 cells.
results.evaluation: Claims C31-C33 transparently document known protocol differences. The injection volume change (C33) is substantial (100-fold difference) and could affect tumor take rate and growth kinetics, though the modification was made on expert advice. Omitting lower doses (C31) reduces ability to assess dose-response but is justified for feasibility.

results.result: All experimental data will be made publicly available through publication or the Open Science Framework.
results.evaluation: Claim C34 describes a clear data sharing plan consistent with open science principles. The commitment to share raw data, analysis, and quality control data enhances reproducibility.

results.result: The statistical analysis plan includes two-way ANOVA (2×2 factorial) with Bonferroni-corrected Welch's t-tests, preceded by normality testing (Shapiro-Wilk, Q-Q plots) and homoscedasticity assessment (Levene's test), with contingency plans for non-normal data and meta-analytic comparison to original results.
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C44 describe a rigorous and appropriate statistical approach. The pre-specification of normality and variance testing (C41-C42) with contingency plans (C43) is methodologically sound. The meta-analytic approach (C44) for comparing original and replication effect sizes is appropriate for replication studies.

results.result: Power calculations using R 3.1.2 and G*Power yielded effect sizes of 1.71 (PBS vs cimetidine) and 2.39 (PBS vs doxorubicin) for A549 xenografts, with planned N=12 per group achieving ≥80% power for pairwise comparisons at Bonferroni-corrected α=0.01678.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C73 provide detailed power calculations, but several issues raise concerns: (1) C67 reports 282.39% power, which is impossible (power cannot exceed 100%), suggesting a calculation or reporting error; (2) C72 notes data were estimated from figures with assumed SEM, introducing potential estimation error; (3) The conversion from SEM to SD (C73) is correct mathematically but compounds any estimation errors; (4) The large effect sizes may be inflated due to small original sample sizes (N=6). These uncertainties affect confidence in the power analysis.

results.result: The replication study proposes to follow mice for 11 days after tumors reach 100 mm³, with unequal sample sizes across cohorts (14 mice for most groups, but only 5 for the doxorubicin control group).
results.evaluation: Reviewers explicitly questioned the experimental design, asking 'Is there a good reason to follow the mice one day short?' (11 vs 12 days) and requesting justification for why 'cohort 2 only has 5 mice while the other 4 cohorts have 14 mice.' These questions indicate uncertainty about the appropriateness of these design choices.

results.result: The statistical analysis plan proposes using two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni corrected Welch's t-tests, with normality and homoscedasticity testing (Shapiro-Wilk and Levene's tests) and contingency plans for data transformation if assumptions are violated.
results.evaluation: Reviewers raised concerns about the statistical approach, stating 'Please make sure that the data do not violate the assumptions of ANOVA: normality and homoscedasiticity' and suggesting 'I suggest the use of contrast within the ANOVA framework instead of t-test if the assumptions of ANOVA are met.' They also recommended using 'two-tailed unequal variance t-test' or 'Wilcoxon rank-sum test' depending on normality, indicating the proposed analysis may need revision.

results.result: The original study demonstrated that cimetidine reduced tumor growth in A549 lung adenocarcinoma xenografts but had no effect on ACHN renal carcinoma xenografts, though conclusions are limited by testing only a single cell line with a single drug.
results.evaluation: While reviewers acknowledged the replication aims to reproduce published results, they explicitly raised concerns about 'the limitation of drawing conclusions for the use of only one cell line, A549,' noting that 'activity of drugs in cell lines and xenografts is generally highly idiosyncratic' and that 'most journals require that any in vitro and in vivo experiments are replicated in multiple cell lines and in vivo models.' This indicates uncertainty about the generalizability of findings from a single cell line.

results.result: Power calculations were performed using R software and G*Power, determining that 12 mice per group would provide 82.4% power overall, with specific effect sizes calculated for each comparison (Glass' delta of 1.71 for cimetidine vs PBS, 2.39 for doxorubicin vs PBS).
results.evaluation: Reviewers noted that 'Power calculation was based on t-test' and suggested alternative statistical approaches, implying the power calculations may need to be revised based on the appropriate statistical test. The reviewers' recommendations for different statistical methods (contrasts within ANOVA, non-parametric tests) suggest uncertainty about whether the current power calculations are based on the most appropriate analysis framework.

results.result: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology aims to replicate 50 cancer biology papers from 2010-2012, including the Sirota et al. study that used computational methods to predict drug repurposing opportunities by comparing gene expression signatures from GEO and the Connectivity Map.
results.evaluation: Reviewers acknowledged the study context without raising concerns, stating 'the authors propose a study to reproduce the findings reported in Figure 4C/D and Supplementary Figure 1 from a previously published manuscript (Sirota et al. Sci Trans Med, 2010).' The background and rationale for the replication were accepted without critique.

results.result: The replication protocol specifies detailed methods for cell culture, xenograft creation, tumor measurement, treatment administration, and data collection, including modifications from the original study (e.g., injecting cells in 100 µl PBS instead of per microliter, excluding lower cimetidine doses).
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about the specific methodological details of cell culture, xenograft procedures, or treatment protocols. Their critiques focused on statistical analysis and experimental design duration/sample sizes rather than these technical procedures, suggesting implicit acceptance of these methodological claims.

results.result: Cimetidine is an H2 receptor blocker used to treat peptic ulcers, and was predicted by Sirota et al. to be effective against lung adenocarcinoma but not renal carcinoma, with some supporting evidence from other studies showing reduced proliferation in vitro and decreased lung cancer risk in epidemiological data.
results.evaluation: Reviewers accepted the background information about cimetidine and the original study's predictions without challenge. They focused their critiques on the experimental design and statistical analysis rather than questioning these foundational claims about the drug and prior findings.

results.result: The replication study will use adaptive randomization for treatment assignment, make all data publicly available on the Open Science Framework, and employ meta-analytic approaches to compare original and replication effect sizes.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about data sharing plans, randomization procedures, or meta-analytic approaches. These methodological elements were not questioned in the review, suggesting implicit acceptance of these aspects of the study design.

results.result: Data extracted from the original study's figures show specific tumor weights at day 11 for each treatment group (e.g., PBS-treated A549: 3.3, cimetidine-treated A549: 2.34), with sample sizes of 6 mice per group, and these values were used to calculate effect sizes using Glass' delta with PBS control SD as the divisor.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question the data extraction methods or the specific values obtained from the original study. Their concerns focused on the statistical analysis plan and experimental design rather than challenging the accuracy of the extracted data or effect size calculations.

comparisons.comparison: Both evaluate statistical analysis claims (C40-C43). OpenEval finds the approach rigorous and appropriate with sound pre-specification of tests. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, questioning whether ANOVA assumptions are met and suggesting alternative tests (contrasts within ANOVA, non-parametric tests), indicating the proposed analysis may need revision.

Both address power calculations (C45-C47, C65-C70). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to impossible 282.39% power value, estimation errors from figure extraction, and potentially inflated effect sizes. Peer reviewers also express uncertainty, noting power calculations were based on t-test and suggesting they may need revision based on alternative statistical approaches.

Both evaluate the original study methodology and rationale (C2, C8-C12). OpenEval finds claims accurate and logically sound but notes the underlying assumption isn't critically evaluated. Peer reviewers support these claims, acknowledging the study context and replication rationale without raising concerns.

Both address project structure claims (C1, C6, C7). OpenEval finds these descriptive claims consistent and supported. Peer reviewers also support these claims as part of accepting the overall study context and background without critique.

Both evaluate methodological details (C21-C30, C52-C57). OpenEval finds comprehensive methods internally consistent and following standard protocols. Peer reviewers implicitly support these technical procedures, focusing critiques elsewhere rather than questioning these methodological claims.

Both address experimental design details (C27, C60-C64). OpenEval supports the comprehensive methodological details as internally consistent. Peer reviewers express uncertainty, explicitly questioning the 11 vs 12 day duration and why cohort 2 has only 5 mice versus 14 in other cohorts, requesting justification for these design choices.

Both evaluate original study results and cell line limitations (C14-C16). OpenEval supports the data extraction and notes C16's valid limitation acknowledgment. Peer reviewers express uncertainty about generalizability from a single cell line, noting drug activity is 'highly idiosyncratic' and most journals require multiple cell lines/models.

Both address experimental limitations (C16). OpenEval supports the limitation acknowledgment as valid given single cell line design. Peer reviewers express stronger uncertainty, explicitly questioning the limitation of using only A549 cells and noting requirements for multiple models.

Both evaluate cimetidine mechanism claims (C3, C13). OpenEval identifies critical pharmacological error (C3 incorrectly states agonist while C13 correctly states blocker) and rates UNSUPPORTED. Peer reviewers support these claims without challenge, accepting the background information about cimetidine.

Both address data extraction from original study (C35-C39, C58-C59). OpenEval supports the specific quantitative data extraction as consistent. Peer reviewers also support these claims, not questioning the accuracy of extracted data or effect size calculations.

Both evaluate supporting studies (C18-C19). OpenEval supports these as providing convergent evidence while noting they use different systems. Peer reviewers accept these background claims without challenge, focusing critiques on experimental design rather than prior findings.

Both address data sharing and meta-analytic plans (C34, C44). OpenEval supports the clear data sharing plan and appropriate meta-analytic approach. Peer reviewers also support these aspects, not raising concerns about data sharing or meta-analysis methods.

Both evaluate protocol differences (C31-C33). OpenEval supports transparent documentation while noting substantial injection volume difference. Peer reviewers implicitly support these methodological details, not raising concerns about the documented protocol deviations.

Both address data extraction and effect size calculations (C71-C73). OpenEval expresses uncertainty due to estimation errors from figures and SEM-to-SD conversion compounding errors. Peer reviewers support the accuracy of extracted values, not questioning the data extraction methods.

Both evaluate original study results (C4-C5). OpenEval supports the consistent description with quantitative data. Peer reviewers also support these claims about the original findings without challenge.
